COLDWAR_SOV_the_doctrine_debate: Since Marshal Sokolovsky's 'Military Strategy' appeared in 1962, Soviet planners have assumed that any war with NATO would turn nuclear within days. A younger generation in the General Staff now argues that massed armour could reach the Rhine before the West dares to escalate. Should the Soviet Army prepare to fight beneath the mushroom cloud, or to win so quickly that the warheads never leave their silos?
COLDWAR_SOV_deep_operations_revived: Rehabilitated along with its author after the purges, Marshal Tukhachevsky's theory of deep operations is returning to the lecture halls of the Frunze Academy. Instead of grinding through NATO's forward defences, successive echelons of tanks and motor rifles would strike across the entire depth of the enemy position at once. By the middle of the decade the idea is once again the guiding star of Soviet operational art.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_nuclear_battlefield: Sokolovsky's school holds that no war in Europe can stay conventional for long, and that the Soviet Army must be built accordingly. Divisions will train to advance through contaminated ground in sealed vehicles, while the rocket troops open the way with tactical warheads. It is a grim doctrine, but one that refuses to pretend the nuclear age never arrived.
COLDWAR_SOV_operational_manoeuvre_groups: Marshal Nikolai Ogarkov and his staff propose a sharper blade for the deep battle: operational manoeuvre groups, powerful tank formations that slip through the first breach and race into NATO's rear before reserves can be committed or nuclear release authorised. Headquarters, airfields and missile sites would fall before the enemy understands what has happened. Speed itself becomes the decisive weapon.
COLDWAR_SOV_theatres_of_military_operati: A war against NATO and China would be fought on several fronts at once, too many for the General Staff in Moscow to direct alone. In 1979 permanent high commands are created for the Western, South-Western, Southern and Far Eastern theatres, each able to control several fronts and fleets in wartime. Command is pushed forward, closer to the battle it must win.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_tank_question: Kharkov's T-64 is the most advanced tank in the world, but it is expensive, temperamental and difficult to build in the numbers a war with NATO would demand. Nizhny Tagil offers a simpler, sturdier machine derived from the same ideas. The defence industry must decide whether the Soviet Army fields a single main battle tank or tolerates two parallel lines of production.
COLDWAR_SOV_t64_morozovs_masterpiece: Alexander Morozov's design bureau in Kharkov has given the Soviet Army a machine years ahead of anything in the West, with composite armour, a powerful smoothbore gun and an automatic loader. Committing fully to the T-64 means accepting its high cost and a complicated engine that keeps the mechanics busy. The elite divisions facing NATO in Germany will receive the finest tank the Union can build.
COLDWAR_SOV_t72_the_mass_tank: Uralvagonzavod in Nizhny Tagil has produced a tank built for the realities of mass war: robust, simple to maintain and cheap enough to equip reserve divisions and allied armies alike. The T-72 will never be the most sophisticated machine on the battlefield, but it can be built in vast numbers and sold across the socialist world. In a long war, quantity has a quality all its own.
COLDWAR_SOV_t80_gas_turbine: The Kirov Plant in Leningrad proposes a radical solution: a tank powered by a gas turbine, giving it the acceleration of a sports car and the thirst of an aircraft. Dmitry Ustinov is an enthusiastic patron, and the T-80 promises a mobility no NATO formation could hope to match. Whether its engines can survive a long winter campaign is a question the engineers must still answer.
COLDWAR_SOV_bmp_infantry_in_armour: The BMP-1 has changed the meaning of infantry. For the first time riflemen can fight from inside an armoured vehicle carrying its own gun and anti-tank missile, keeping pace with the tanks even across contaminated ground. Building tactics and production around the infantry fighting vehicle will give every motor rifle regiment the protection and firepower the modern battlefield demands.
COLDWAR_SOV_ak74: The Kalashnikov has armed half the world, but its heavy cartridge is a relic of the Second World War. Izhmash has developed a lighter weapon firing a small-calibre, high-velocity round that is more accurate at range and lets each soldier carry more ammunition. Adopted in 1974, the AK-74 will become the standard rifle of the Soviet Army for decades to come.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_praporshchiki: The conscript army turns over every two years, and the gap between raw recruits and their officers has long been filled by no one. In 1972 the rank of praporshchik is introduced: long-serving professional warrant officers who manage stores, vehicles and discipline at company level. They cost more than conscripts, but they give the Soviet Army a backbone of experience it has always lacked.
COLDWAR_SOV_against_dedovshchina: In the barracks, second-year conscripts, the so-called 'grandfathers', rule over the newcomers through beatings, extortion and humiliation that officers prefer not to see. Breaking this unwritten hierarchy means prosecuting the tormentors, punishing commanders who look away and admitting that the problem exists at all. The generals resent the interference, but an army that preys on itself cannot fight well.
COLDWAR_SOV_margelovs_airborne: General Vasily Margelov has turned the Airborne Troops into an elite force, with their striped vests, blue berets and air-dropped armoured vehicles. Soldiers already call them 'Uncle Vasya's Troops'. Raising the airborne divisions to a strategic reserve of the High Command would give Moscow a force able to seize capitals, airfields and bridgeheads anywhere within reach of the transport fleet.
COLDWAR_SOV_spetsnaz_of_the_gru: Military intelligence maintains its own special purpose brigades, small teams trained to parachute deep behind enemy lines, locate NATO's tactical nuclear weapons and destroy them before they can be used. Expanding the Spetsnaz of the GRU would give every front a hidden sword in the enemy's rear. Their very existence remains a closely guarded secret, even within the Soviet Army itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_mi24_the_flying_tank: Mil's design bureau has created something without parallel: a heavily armoured gunship that can also carry a squad of infantry into battle. The Mi-24 combines rockets, cannon and anti-tank missiles with the speed to strike anywhere along the front. Soldiers already call it the 'flying tank', and its silhouette will soon become one of the most feared in the world.
COLDWAR_SOV_rocket_artillery: The legacy of the wartime Katyusha lives on in the Grad, a truck-mounted launcher able to saturate an entire grid square in seconds. Its heavier successor, the Uragan, is already being designed to strike targets far behind the front. Massing rocket artillery would give Soviet commanders the crushing firepower needed to blast open NATO's defences ahead of the armoured breakthrough.
COLDWAR_SOV_universal_military_duty: The 1967 Law on Universal Military Duty shortened service to two years but made it truly universal, backed by pre-conscription training in schools and by the volunteer society DOSAAF. Every young Soviet man is meant to arrive at his unit already able to shoot, drive and read a map. The army gains a deep pool of trained reserves, and society learns to see service as a debt owed to the Motherland.
COLDWAR_SOV_ustinovs_ministry: In 1976 the death of Marshal Grechko brings Dmitry Ustinov to the Ministry of Defence, a lifelong manager of the armaments industry rather than a field commander. Ustinov knows every factory and design bureau personally, and under him weapons will flow faster and cheaper than ever before. The professional soldiers grumble that an industrialist, not a general, now runs the Soviet Army.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_army_of_a_superpower: A generation after Victory, the Soviet Army stands as the largest and most powerful land force on earth, with divisions deployed from the Elbe to the Amur. Its officers are well trained, its arsenals full and its doctrine studied by friend and foe alike. Now it must prove that it is more than a parade on Red Square: a force ready to win any war the Motherland may be forced to fight.
COLDWAR_SOV_strategic_rocket_forces: Created by Khrushchev in 1959, the Strategic Rocket Forces have become the senior service of the Soviet military, guardians of the missiles that can reach any point on the globe. Their silos stretch from Belorussia to the Siberian taiga. Investing in new generations of intercontinental missiles will ensure that the Soviet Union can never again be blackmailed by American nuclear superiority.
COLDWAR_SOV_nuclear_parity: For the first time in history, the Soviet Union possesses as many intercontinental missiles as the United States. The humiliation of Cuba in 1962 has been answered by a decade of relentless construction, and Washington must now negotiate with Moscow as an equal. Parity brings confidence to the Kremlin, but also a new and dangerous temptation to believe that any confrontation can be won.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_heavy_icbm: The Yuzhnoye design bureau in Dnepropetrovsk is preparing the R-36M, a missile so large that it can carry ten warheads or a single devastating charge. In the West it will be called the SS-18 'Satan', and its accuracy threatens the American Minuteman silos themselves. Deploying it would give the Soviet Union a genuine first-strike capability, and Washington will see it exactly that way.
COLDWAR_SOV_mirv_and_mobile_launchers: Fixed silos can be targeted, and every year American missiles grow more accurate. Some designers argue that survivability matters more than sheer numbers: several independently targeted warheads on every missile, and launchers that roam the roads and railways where no satellite can follow them. A smaller arsenal that cannot be destroyed in a first strike may deter more effectively than a larger one that can.
COLDWAR_SOV_pioneer_the_ss20: The ageing missiles aimed at Western Europe can be replaced by the RSD-10 Pioneer, a mobile and accurate weapon carrying three warheads. NATO will call it the SS-20, and it can hold every capital from London to Rome hostage without ever threatening America itself. It would give Moscow a powerful lever over Europe, but it may also provoke Bonn and its allies into a dangerous response.
COLDWAR_SOV_pvo_strany: Unlike any Western nation, the Soviet Union treats the defence of its own airspace as a separate branch of the armed forces. PVO Strany commands the radars, interceptor regiments and missile batteries stretching from the Baltic to the Pacific coast. Strengthening it will ensure that no American bomber or spy plane crosses the Soviet border without paying for it, as Gary Powers learned in 1960.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_moscow_shield: Around the capital the A-35 anti-ballistic missile system is finally entering service, with enormous radars and interceptors designed to destroy incoming warheads high above the atmosphere. It cannot stop a full American attack, but it can protect the leadership against a limited strike or an accidental launch. Completing the shield will be expensive, and it may yet become a bargaining chip in future arms control talks.
COLDWAR_SOV_frontal_aviation: Frontal Aviation is the air arm that fights alongside the ground forces, clearing the skies above the tank columns and striking NATO airfields, bridges and nuclear launchers. Its regiments in East Germany and Czechoslovakia stand only minutes from the inner German border. Refining its tactics and training will turn the air force into a true partner of the deep operation rather than a separate war fought overhead.
COLDWAR_SOV_swing_wings: Variable-geometry wings promise the best of both worlds: short take-offs from rough forward airfields and high speed at low level. Mikoyan's MiG-23 is set to become the workhorse fighter of the Warsaw Pact, while Sukhoi's Su-24 can penetrate deep into Western Europe at treetop height, by night and in any weather. Together they will carry Frontal Aviation into a new decade.
COLDWAR_SOV_mig25_foxbat: Designed to catch an American supersonic bomber that was never built, the MiG-25 can race at nearly three times the speed of sound at the edge of the stratosphere. No Western fighter can catch it and few missiles can reach it. Pressing it into service as an interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft would give the air defence forces a weapon that truly lives up to its legend.
COLDWAR_SOV_long_range_aviation: The strategic bombers of Long-Range Aviation have long lived in the shadow of the rocket forces. Tupolev's Tu-22M, known in the West as the 'Backfire', promises to change that: a supersonic swing-wing bomber able to strike carrier groups at sea and targets across Europe and Asia. Whether it could also reach America will become a fierce question at every arms control table.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_fourth_generation: The American F-15 and F-16 have set a new standard in the air, and Soviet designers are determined to answer them. Sukhoi's Su-27 promises long range and extraordinary agility, while Mikoyan's MiG-29 will be a nimble frontline fighter for the whole Warsaw Pact. Accelerating both programmes would give the Soviet Air Force aircraft capable of matching, perhaps surpassing, anything the West can field.
COLDWAR_SOV_civil_defence_of_the_ussr: Civil Defence of the USSR teaches every schoolchild to put on a gas mask and every factory to prepare its shelters. Deep metro stations double as bunkers, and evacuation plans exist for every major city. Expanding the programme reassures the population that the state has prepared for the worst, and signals to Washington that the Soviet Union intends to survive even a nuclear war.
COLDWAR_SOV_strategic_superiority: At the Twenty-Fifth Party Congress in 1976, Brezhnev declares that the correlation of forces in the world has shifted decisively in favour of socialism. Nuclear parity, the American defeat in Vietnam and revolutions across Africa all seem to prove him right. Embracing this confidence turns caution into assertiveness, but the West may well read Soviet optimism as a threat to be countered.
COLDWAR_SOV_gorshkovs_navy: Admiral Sergei Gorshkov has commanded the Soviet Navy since 1956, and he has a vision: a fleet able to sail every ocean and show the red flag wherever the Americans go. Coastal defence is no longer enough for a superpower. Under his guidance new cruisers, submarines and replenishment ships are turning a navy built for home waters into a true ocean-going fleet.
COLDWAR_SOV_okean_70: In April 1970 the Soviet Navy stages Okean, the largest naval exercise since the Second World War. Ships of the Northern, Baltic, Black Sea and Pacific Fleets manoeuvre simultaneously across the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Mediterranean, rehearsing the destruction of American carrier groups. The message to Washington is unmistakable: the oceans no longer belong to the West alone.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_navy_question: Admiral Gorshkov preaches that a superpower needs a balanced fleet, yet resources are finite and the admirals are divided into two camps. One side wants submarines above all, cheap to hide and deadly against carriers and convoys. The other dreams of carriers and great surface ships able to project Soviet power to distant shores. The Party must decide what kind of sea power the state requires.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_submarine_fleet: Submarines are the great equaliser of the Soviet Navy. Hunter-killer boats can stalk American carriers and convoys, while missile submarines carry a share of the nuclear deterrent that no enemy can find and destroy. Concentrating the shipyards on the underwater fleet will give the Soviet Union the largest submarine force in the world and a nuclear arsenal hidden beneath the waves.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_bastion_strategy: Rather than sending missile submarines into the open Atlantic, where American hunters lie in wait, the Navy can keep them close to home. The Barents Sea and the Sea of Okhotsk would become protected bastions, guarded by surface ships, aircraft and attack submarines. From these sanctuaries new long-range missiles could still reach the United States, while the boats themselves remain safe.
COLDWAR_SOV_lira_the_titanium_submarine: Project 705, which NATO will call the Alfa, is a submarine unlike any other: a titanium hull, a liquid-metal reactor and a crew so small that automation replaces most of its sailors. It can outrun almost any torpedo in the Western arsenal and dive deeper than its pursuers. The cost is staggering and the reactor temperamental, but no other navy on earth could build such a vessel.
COLDWAR_SOV_akula_the_typhoon: The Rubin design bureau proposes the largest submarine ever built: Project 941 Akula, which the West will call the Typhoon. With a hull broad and strong enough to break through Arctic ice, it could surface near the North Pole and launch its missiles at America. Building such giants will strain the yards of Severodvinsk, but they would make the naval deterrent virtually invulnerable.
COLDWAR_SOV_carriers_and_cruisers: Submarines can sink a fleet, but they cannot show the flag or support allies in distant waters. A balanced fleet of aircraft-carrying cruisers and heavy missile cruisers would let the Soviet Union project power from the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean. The yards of Nikolaev and Leningrad stand ready, if the Party is willing to pay for a true ocean-going surface navy.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_kiev_class: The Black Sea Shipyard in Nikolaev is preparing a new type of warship: the heavy aircraft-carrying cruiser. The Kiev class combines vertical take-off jets and helicopters with heavy anti-ship missiles, and as a 'cruiser' it can legally pass through the Turkish Straits. It is not yet a true aircraft carrier, but it is the first step toward one.
COLDWAR_SOV_kirov_the_battlecruiser: Project 1144, the Kirov class, would be the largest surface combatant built anywhere since the Second World War: a nuclear-powered battlecruiser bristling with anti-ship and anti-aircraft missiles. Its purpose is to lead surface action groups against American carriers and to shield Soviet submarines on their way to sea. Its sheer size announces that the Soviet Navy has come of age.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_fifth_eskadra: The Fifth Operational Squadron keeps Soviet warships permanently in the Mediterranean, shadowing the American Sixth Fleet and showing support for Arab allies. To stay at sea it needs friendly harbours for supplies and repairs. Moscow will ask Damascus for a naval supply point at Tartus, an arrangement that could give the Soviet Union a lasting foothold on the Mediterranean coast.
COLDWAR_SOV_naval_missile_aviation: Naval Missile Aviation is the long arm of Gorshkov's fleet: regiments of land-based bombers armed with heavy anti-ship missiles. Their task is to find American carrier groups far out at sea and overwhelm them with massed missile strikes before their aircraft can threaten the Soviet coast. Expanding this force is the most economical way to challenge American dominance of the oceans.
COLDWAR_SOV_bases_on_three_oceans: A global navy needs global harbours. Berbera in Somalia and Aden in South Yemen overlook the gateway between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean, while Cam Ranh Bay in Vietnam looks out over the South China Sea. Moscow will offer its partners aid and protection in exchange for port rights, but no ally will be forced to accept the offer.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_shipyards_of_the_north: Every ship of the ocean-going fleet must first be built, and the great yards are already working at the limit of their capacity. Severodvinsk on the White Sea launches the nuclear submarines, while Nikolaev on the Black Sea produces the large surface ships. Expanding both will ensure that the ambitions of the admirals are not frustrated by a simple shortage of slipways.
COLDWAR_SOV_a_navy_of_a_superpower: Where once the Soviet Navy hugged the coastline, its ships now sail every ocean on earth. Squadrons patrol the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, and Soviet flags fly in harbours from Havana to Aden. Gorshkov's dream has become reality: a true blue-water navy, the equal of any fleet that sails the seas.
COLDWAR_SOV_andropovs_kgb: Since 1967 Yuri Andropov has led the Committee for State Security, and he has transformed it. Gone are the crude terror methods of the Stalin years; in their place stands a modern, professional service relying on surveillance, informers and the quiet pressure of 'prophylactic' conversations. Andropov is intelligent, ambitious and trusted by Brezhnev, and his KGB is becoming a pillar of the state.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_fifth_directorate: Created on Andropov's initiative in 1967, the Fifth Directorate of the KGB is tasked with combating 'ideological subversion'. Its officers watch writers, churches, national movements and anyone who listens too closely to foreign radio. Expanding its reach will help the Party detect dissent before it can spread, though every new file deepens the silence that hangs over Soviet intellectual life.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_dissident_question: Since the trial of Sinyavsky and Daniel in 1966, a small but stubborn dissident movement has taken shape. Samizdat manuscripts circulate from hand to hand, Andrei Sakharov speaks out for human rights, and Solzhenitsyn's novels reach the world through foreign publishers. The state must decide whether to crush these voices, expel them, or quietly allow them a space to exist.
COLDWAR_SOV_punitive_psychiatry: If opposing Soviet power is a sign of madness, then dissidents belong in hospitals rather than prisons. Psychiatrists of the Serbsky Institute have developed a convenient diagnosis, 'sluggish schizophrenia', that can be applied to anyone who refuses to conform. The special psychiatric hospitals will silence the troublemakers, but the West will condemn the practice as a grotesque abuse of medicine.
COLDWAR_SOV_exile_and_expulsion: Neither prison nor tolerance: the most troublesome voices can simply be removed. Solzhenitsyn, after the publication of 'The Gulag Archipelago' abroad, can be stripped of his citizenship and put on a plane to the West, while Sakharov can be banished to the closed city of Gorky. The dissidents lose their audience at home, though they gain a far louder one abroad.
COLDWAR_SOV_tolerate_the_samizdat: What if the Party decided that typewritten manuscripts and private poetry readings posed no real threat to socialism? Tolerating samizdat would let new ideas circulate among scientists and intellectuals and soften the hostility of Western opinion. The KGB warns that tolerance is the first step toward another Prague Spring, but reformers argue that a confident socialism need not fear mere words.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_refusenik_question: Since the Six-Day War, thousands of Soviet Jews have applied to emigrate to Israel, and many have been refused, losing their jobs and becoming 'refuseniks'. In Washington, Senator Henry Jackson seeks to link American trade benefits to the freedom to emigrate. The Kremlin must decide whether to open the gates for the sake of detente or to hold on to the specialists it has trained.
COLDWAR_SOV_open_the_gates: Letting those who wish to leave depart would remove a constant irritant from relations with the United States and unlock the trade and credits the economy needs. It also means watching engineers, doctors and scientists board trains and planes for Vienna and onward to Israel. The Politburo weighs the loss of talent against the benefits of detente, and chooses to let them go.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_diploma_tax: In August 1972 the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet decrees that emigrants must repay the cost of their state education before they may leave. For a university graduate the sum can equal many years of wages. The measure brings in hard currency and discourages the drain of talent, but it provokes outrage in the West and threatens the trade deals of detente.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_first_chief_directorate: The First Chief Directorate of the KGB runs Soviet intelligence abroad. Its officers work under diplomatic cover in embassies, trade missions and news agencies, recruiting sources in governments, armies and laboratories around the world. Expanding its networks and its codebreakers will give the Kremlin the secrets it needs to stay one step ahead of its rivals.
COLDWAR_SOV_active_measures: Service A of the First Chief Directorate specialises in 'active measures': forged documents, planted newspaper stories and quiet support for peace movements and friendly politicians in the West. Its aim is not to steal secrets but to shape opinion, sow distrust between Washington and its allies, and make the Soviet cause appear to be the cause of peace itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_illegals: The most valuable agents carry no diplomatic passport at all. The illegals live for years under false identities in the West as shopkeepers, engineers or academics, waiting for the moment they are needed. Training them takes years and losing one is a disaster, but a well-placed illegal can reach places no embassy officer ever could, and vanish without a trace.
COLDWAR_SOV_kgb_border_troops: The KGB Border Troops guard the longest frontier in the world, from the Baltic coast to the Pacific, from the Arctic tundra to the mountains of Central Asia. After the bloody clashes with China on the Ussuri in 1969, their importance is clearer than ever. Strengthening the border guards will keep foreign agents out, smugglers in check and Soviet citizens safely at home.
COLDWAR_SOV_operation_ryan: The leadership of the KGB has become convinced that the Americans are preparing a surprise nuclear attack. Operation RYaN, an acronym for 'nuclear missile attack' in Russian, orders every KGB and GRU station abroad to watch for warning signs: lights burning late at the Pentagon, blood banks filling up, officials cancelling their holidays. The hunt for the first strike may save the nation, or push the world to the brink.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_anti_corruption_drive: Corruption has spread through the Party and the state like rot through timber. Ministers protect their clients, regional leaders run their territories as personal fiefdoms, and goods vanish from factories into the black market. A determined campaign of arrests and investigations would restore discipline, but it will make powerful enemies among a nomenklatura that has grown comfortable under the stability of cadres.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_shield_and_the_sword: Since the days of Dzerzhinsky, the Chekists have called themselves the shield and the sword of the Party. Under this banner the KGB can bind its many tasks into a single purpose, from counter-intelligence at home to guarding the borders and watching for ideological subversion. A security service at the height of its power makes the Soviet state very difficult to undermine from within or without.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_union_of_republics: The Soviet Union is a federation of fifteen republics, each with its own Party, government and flag. Behind the slogans of the friendship of peoples lie real tensions: national elites seeking autonomy, Russians resentful of subsidising the periphery, and a population growing fastest in the south. Moscow must learn to manage the Union as carefully as it manages the economy.
COLDWAR_SOV_local_barons_or_moscows_men: Brezhnev's 'stability of cadres' has left powerful first secretaries in charge of the republics for years: Kunaev in Kazakhstan, Rashidov in Uzbekistan, Shcherbytsky in Ukraine. They deliver loyalty and plan figures, and in return Moscow leaves them largely alone. Should the Kremlin continue to trust these local barons, or send its own men to keep watch over them?
COLDWAR_SOV_trust_the_local_barons: The bargain is simple: the republican leaders keep their territories quiet, vote with Brezhnev in the Politburo and meet their plans, at least on paper. In exchange Moscow asks few questions about how they run their domains. The Union will be calmer and more cohesive, even if corruption and nepotism flourish behind the facades of Tashkent, Alma-Ata and Baku.
COLDWAR_SOV_rotate_the_cadres: Trust is good, but control is better. Moscow will place Russian second secretaries in every republican Party organisation, rotate officials between regions and break up the local networks that shield corrupt leaders. The republics will resent the outsiders, but no first secretary will ever again be able to treat his republic as a personal possession.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_ukrainian_question: Ukraine is the second pillar of the Union, home to vital industries, rich farmland and a large and proud nation. Its first secretary, Petro Shelest, defends Ukrainian culture and the republic's economic interests, sometimes too openly for Moscow's liking. The Kremlin must decide whether to tolerate Shelest's course or replace it with something more reliably loyal.
COLDWAR_SOV_shelests_ukraine: What if Petro Shelest had kept his post? His book 'Our Soviet Ukraine' celebrates the republic's history and its Cossack traditions, and his leadership shields the Ukrainian language and intelligentsia. A Ukraine secure in its identity may prove a more willing partner in the Union, though some in Moscow fear it could also become a far more demanding one.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_shcherbytsky_line: In 1972 Shelest is removed and Volodymyr Shcherbytsky, a close ally of Brezhnev, takes over in Kiev. Shelest's book is condemned as nationalist, and a wave of arrests sweeps through the Ukrainian intelligentsia while Russian gains ground in schools and publishing. Ukraine becomes a model of loyalty, but the resentment buried in those years does not simply disappear.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_baltic_question: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are the most prosperous and Western-minded republics of the Union, with high living standards, a strong sense of national identity and long memories of independence. They can serve as a showcase of what socialism can achieve, or as a laboratory for deeper integration with the rest of the country. Moscow must choose how to treat its western frontier.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_soviet_west: Let the Baltic republics be the shop window of socialism. Tallinn's designers, the fashion houses of Riga and the cafes of Vilnius can show visitors, and the rest of the Union, that Soviet life can be modern and stylish. Estonians already watch Finnish television across the gulf; allowing them a little more freedom may win more loyalty than any campaign of Russification.
COLDWAR_SOV_industrial_migration: New industrial combines in Riga and Tallinn need workers, and the Baltic republics cannot supply enough of them. Bringing in labour from Russia, Ukraine and Belorussia will boost production and tie the region more closely to the Union. Yet every new apartment block filled with Russian-speaking workers feeds the fear among Latvians and Estonians that they are becoming minorities in their own lands.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_caucasus: Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan form the southern frontier of the Union, a region of ancient nations, fierce pride and old rivalries. Their economies thrive on private plots and the shadow market as much as on the plan, and their Party bosses are among the most corrupt in the country. Bringing order to Transcaucasia will require both a firm hand and a careful touch.
COLDWAR_SOV_shevardnadze_cleans_tbilisi: In 1972 Eduard Shevardnadze, the Georgian minister of internal affairs, replaces the discredited Vasil Mzhavanadze as first secretary in Tbilisi. He launches a sweeping campaign against bribery and the black market, purging thousands of officials. Georgians are astonished, Moscow is impressed, and the ambitious new leader begins a career that may take him far beyond the Caucasus.
COLDWAR_SOV_aliyev_in_baku: Heydar Aliyev, a career KGB officer, has led Azerbaijan since 1969. He presents himself as a scourge of corruption while building a network of loyal clans, and he flatters Brezhnev lavishly on every visit. Under his rule the oil industry of Baku is modernised and the republic reports spectacular growth. Backing Aliyev buys stability on the Caspian, at a price that is never written down.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_karabakh_petitions: The Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh, an autonomous region inside Azerbaijan, have petitioned Moscow for decades to be transferred to Armenia, and each time the request is quietly buried. Granting it would satisfy Yerevan but enrage Baku; refusing it preserves the status quo while the grievance festers. Historically, this very question would begin to tear the Union apart in 1988.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_central_asian_barons: In Central Asia, Kunaev in Kazakhstan and Rashidov in Uzbekistan rule with an almost feudal authority. Their republics deliver cotton, grain and unwavering loyalty, and in return Moscow tolerates their clans, their courts of flatterers and their creative accounting. The arrangement keeps the region calm, but the Kremlin knows less and less about what really happens in Tashkent and Alma-Ata.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_cotton_affair: Uzbekistan reports record cotton harvests year after year, and Moscow pays billions of roubles for them. But investigators suspect that much of this cotton exists only on paper, with the difference pocketed by a pyramid of officials reaching all the way to the top of the republic. Exposing the fraud would strike a mighty blow against corruption, but it will humiliate an entire republic.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_language_question: More than a hundred languages are spoken across the Soviet Union, and the question of which should be taught in schools is never merely educational. Russian binds together the Union, the army and the economy, but the national languages carry the identity of each people. Moscow must decide how far to promote Russian and how much room to leave for the native tongues.
COLDWAR_SOV_russian_as_lingua_franca: A decree of 1978 strengthens the teaching of Russian from the very first grade in every school of the Union, praising it as the language of inter-ethnic communication. Conscripts from Tashkent to Tallinn will understand their officers, and engineers can move freely between the republics. Yet when Georgia's language rights are threatened that same year, crowds fill the streets of Tbilisi in protest.
COLDWAR_SOV_native_language_schools: Rather than forcing Russian into every classroom, the Party could guarantee schooling in the native language of each republic, with Russian taught as a second tongue. National intelligentsias would welcome the gesture, and the friendship of peoples would sound less like Russification. The army complains that recruits arrive unable to follow orders, but loyalty freely given may be worth more.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_union_treaty_question: The Union Treaty of 1922 bound the republics together, but the state it created is now groaning under the weight of national demands, economic strain and political doubt. If the bonds begin to weaken, Moscow must choose: renegotiate the Union as a voluntary federation of sovereign states, or hold it together through sheer force of will and arms.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_renewed_federation: A new treaty could transform the Soviet Union into a genuine federation of sovereign republics, with real powers over their economies, languages and cultures, united by a common defence, currency and foreign policy. The hardliners see it as the beginning of the end. The reformers answer that a union held together by consent is the only union that can truly last.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_iron_union: There will be no new treaty and no negotiation with nationalists. The Union was forged in revolution and war and will be preserved by the same means: the KGB will watch the national movements, the army will stand ready, and any first secretary who flirts with separatism will be removed. Order will be maintained, but at the cost of the goodwill of millions.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_soviet_people_realised: The Party has long proclaimed the emergence of a new historical community: the Soviet people, bound together not by blood or language but by shared ideals and a common future. With the Union secured, this promise may finally become reality, as Uzbeks, Ukrainians and Latvians come to see themselves as Soviet citizens first and foremost.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_soviet_way_of_life: Guaranteed work, cheap bread, free healthcare and a separate apartment for every family: this is the promise of the Soviet way of life. For millions who remember the war and the crowded communal flats, these are the best years they have ever known. Celebrating these achievements reminds the people what they owe to socialism, and what they stand to lose.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_alcohol_problem: Vodka is woven into every celebration, every bargain and every tragedy of Soviet life. Consumption keeps climbing year after year, and alcoholism fills the hospitals, empties the factories and shortens the lives of Soviet men. Yet the sale of alcohol also fills the state treasury. The Party must decide whether it can afford to fight the bottle, or afford not to.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_vodka_monopoly: The state monopoly on vodka brings in a huge share of all retail revenue, money the budget simply cannot do without. Rather than fighting the national vice, the Ministry of Finance will quietly profit from it. Hospitals and factories will pay the price in absent workers and ruined health, but as long as the shelves are stocked, the people remain content.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_1972_temperance_decree: In 1972 the Central Committee resolves to combat drunkenness and alcoholism, restricting opening hours, raising prices and cutting the production of strong spirits. Enforced seriously, the decree could save lives and lift labour productivity, though the treasury will lose a vital source of income. Many citizens will simply turn to home-distilled samogon, and their goodwill toward the Party may suffer.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_sporting_superpower: From the Olympic podium to the ice hockey rink, the chessboard and the football pitch, Soviet athletes prove the strength of socialism to the whole world. Sports schools search for talent in every town and village, and champions become national heroes. Investing in sport costs little compared to missiles, yet every gold medal is a small victory in the Cold War.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_moscow_olympics: In 1974 the International Olympic Committee awards the 1980 Summer Games to Moscow, the first Olympics ever to be held in a socialist country. New stadiums, hotels and an Olympic village must be built, and the capital polished for the eyes of the world. The Games promise a triumph of Soviet prestige, unless the West decides to stay away.
COLDWAR_SOV_culture_question: The cultural thaw of the Khrushchev years is long over, but it has never been fully reversed. Writers, filmmakers and theatre directors test the limits of what the censors will allow, and audiences flock to anything that hints at forbidden truths. The Party must decide whether to tighten its grip on culture or to permit a carefully managed openness.
COLDWAR_SOV_glavlit_holds_the_line: Glavlit, the central censorship office, reviews every book, newspaper and film before it reaches the public. Under firm instructions from the ideological apparatus, it will continue to cut, delay and ban anything that strays from the Party line. Soviet culture will remain safely orthodox, while its most gifted artists either conform, fall silent or turn to samizdat.
COLDWAR_SOV_cultural_detente: Lyubimov's Taganka Theatre stages daring productions, Vysotsky's songs play on tape recorders in every apartment block, and Tarkovsky films masterpieces that the censors struggle to understand. What if the Party chose to tolerate rather than suppress them? A measure of cultural freedom could reconcile the intelligentsia with the state and show the world a more human face of socialism.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_church_question: Despite decades of persecution, the Russian Orthodox Church endures, as do Muslim, Catholic, Baptist and Jewish communities across the Union. The Council for Religious Affairs keeps believers under close watch, and attending church is a risk for anyone with a career. The Party must decide whether to intensify the struggle against religion or to seek a quiet accommodation with it.
COLDWAR_SOV_scientific_atheism: Religion is a relic of the past, destined to disappear as society advances toward communism. Lectures, museums of atheism and the Znanie Society will carry the scientific worldview into every town and village, while the authorities continue to restrict new parishes and the training of clergy. Believers will grow fewer in public, even if many continue to pray in private.
COLDWAR_SOV_accord_with_the_patriarchate: What if the Party sought a genuine partnership with the Moscow Patriarchate rather than merely tolerating it? Loosening the restrictions on parishes and seminaries could win the gratitude of millions of believers and turn the Church into an ally in patriotic and peace campaigns. Hardline ideologues are appalled, but the Church may prove a valuable pillar of stability.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_double_burden: Soviet women make up more than half of the workforce, serving as doctors, engineers and crane operators. Yet when their shift ends a second one begins: queues for groceries, cooking, laundry and childcare, with little help from husbands or the economy. Easing this double burden through more kindergartens, services and household goods would improve countless lives and keep women at work.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_demographic_gap: In Russia and the Baltic republics most families have one or two children, while in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan they have five or six. The demographic centre of the Union is shifting steadily southward, toward Central Asia and the Caucasus. Planners must adapt by building schools and jobs in the south, encouraging larger families in the north and preparing an army whose recruits speak less and less Russian.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_developed_socialist_soci: Brezhnev's ideologists declare that the Soviet Union has reached the stage of 'developed socialism', a mature society on the road to communism, and the new constitution of 1977 enshrines the claim. If it can be made real, with rising living standards and a confident population, the socialist way of life may become an example the whole world wishes to follow.
COLDWAR_SOV_peaceful_coexistence: Lenin's principle of peaceful coexistence holds that socialism and capitalism can compete without war. In the age of nuclear parity, the Kremlin sees a chance to turn the principle into practice through arms control talks, trade with the West and the recognition of the post-war order in Europe. Detente will not end the struggle between the systems, but it may move it to safer ground.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_moscow_treaty: Chancellor Willy Brandt's new eastern policy offers an opportunity that seemed impossible only a few years ago. A treaty between the Soviet Union and West Germany would renounce the use of force and recognise the post-war borders of Europe, including the Oder-Neisse line. Moscow is ready to make the offer; Bonn must decide whether to sign it.
